title: Everyone Hears It

post.author: u/flood_desk_ceinwen
post.title: I'm the night duty officer at a river town's flood warning office. Our sirens warned the town 73 seconds after the water was already in the square.

blocks.text: I keep the night desk at the flood warning office in Ollerby, a river town on the Quarrow. Upstream there's a gauge that measures the river, and a program Florimond, our developer, wrote years ago: the gauge service. When the river crosses its warning level, the gauge service warns the town on four alert channels: a text (SMS) to every phone signed up, a banner on our website, the town's sirens, and Quarrow Sound, the local radio station, which breaks into whatever is playing. Each one is a call. The gauge service asks a channel to send and waits for its answer before it calls the next: SMS, website, sirens, radio. Florimond calls it the chain.
It had never been slow. It had never needed to be fast.

On Tuesday night the river crossed the level at 02:31. The siren mast is across the road from my window, and I stood up to watch it. It stayed silent. At about 02:33 the river came over the wall into Doveridge Square, the lowest part of town, where people leave their cars overnight. The sirens started at 02:34. By then the water was round the wheels.

02:31:00  gauge-svc      level crossed warning: calling sms
02:32:50  square-sensor  water on the paving
02:34:00  gauge-svc      sms: no answer, timed out after 180 s
02:34:00  gauge-svc      calling website
02:34:01  gauge-svc      website: ok
02:34:01  gauge-svc      calling sirens
02:34:03  gauge-svc      sirens: ok
02:34:03  gauge-svc      calling radio
02:34:04  gauge-svc      radio: ok
02:38:02  gauge-svc      sms: ok (try 3)

Nobody was hurt. Cars and cellars flooded. The texts reached phones at 02:38, when people were already standing in their cellars in wet socks. Florimond pulled the logs. The SMS provider had hung, and the gauge service waited the full 180-second timeout for an answer that never came, with the sirens waiting their turn behind it. The provider says it was back by 02:37.
The siren log says it warned the town after the square's own sensor says the water was already there.

blocks.label: warning_0231.png

diagram.aria: Tuesday from 02:31:00 to 02:39:00. The SMS call hangs from 02:31:00 to 02:34:00, is tried again from 02:34:30 to 02:37:30 and hangs again, and goes through at 02:38:00. The website waits until 02:34:00 and is updated at 02:34:01. The sirens wait until 02:34:01 and sound at 02:34:03. The radio waits until 02:34:03 and is on air at 02:34:04. Water is on the low square from 02:32:50.

blocks.caption: Florimond's logs for Tuesday, redrawn. The SMS call hung from 02:31:00 until its timeout at 02:34:00, and everything after it in the chain waited. The square's sensor saw water at 02:32:50; the sirens sounded at 02:34:03, 73 seconds later. The texts went at 02:38:02, on the third try.

blocks.text: Florimond has four changes on the board. The river will be high again before the winter is out. Which one do we make?

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Some words first. A call means one program asks another and waits for the answer; your chain is four calls in a row, so each channel waits for every one before it. A thread is a separate line of work inside one program, so one program can make several calls at once. Publish and subscribe, pub/sub for short, works the other way round: a program publishes a message to a topic, a named place for one kind of message, and each subscriber to the topic gets its own copy. The publisher doesn't know who they are. Now the evidence. What were the sirens doing between 02:31:00 and 02:34:01? When the SMS call failed, which program remembered that the text still had to go, and where did it keep that? And what would have happened to that memory if the program had restarted at 02:32?

replies.author: u/flood_desk_ceinwen
replies.text: Florimond says the sirens did nothing at all until 02:34:01. They were never asked. The gauge service keeps its list of channels still to try again in its own memory. It restarted once last spring for an automatic update, he says, on a dry night, so nobody noticed.

comments.author: u/siren_first_grimwade
comments.text: Just put the sirens first. It's one line: move the siren call to the top of the list. The sirens are the channel that wakes a whole street; a text is a nice extra. Replay your own night with the sirens first and they sound at 02:31:02, nearly two minutes before the water. The chain has worked for years. Don't rebuild a working system over one slow text provider.

comments.author: u/cellar_tibbott
comments.text: I live just off Doveridge Square. My phone buzzed with the flood warning at 02:38. I was already in the cellar with a torch and the water over my boots, reading it.

reply.prompt: Florimond can make one change before the river is high again. Which should it be? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Move the sirens to the front of the chain, so the call that matters most is never left waiting.
options.verdict: Sirens on time, the rest still wait
options.part2: Florimond moved the siren call to the top of the list and replayed Tuesday in his lab. The sirens sounded at 02:31:02, 108 seconds before the water. Then the SMS call hung, exactly as before, and the rest of the chain waited behind it: the website at 02:34:03, the radio at 02:34:04, the texts at 02:38:04. Three of the four channels still after the water. Then he replayed it with the siren controller hanging instead of the SMS provider. The siren call timed out at 02:34:00, the texts went at 02:34:02, the website at 02:34:03, the radio at 02:34:04, and the sirens themselves at 02:38:02, on their third try. Every channel after the water. In January the siren controller's line did hang, on a night the river was rising. I sat at the desk and watched our website show no warning at all for three minutes, because it was waiting its turn behind a siren that wasn't answering.
options.senior: Reordering a chain chooses which channel goes first; it doesn't stop one slow channel holding up the rest. Whatever sits first can hang, and then everything behind it waits the full timeout. The channels have to stop sharing one line of calls, so that each succeeds or fails on its own.

options.text: Have the gauge service call all four channels at once, each in its own thread, so none waits.
options.verdict: Fast, until the gauge service restarts
options.part2: Florimond gave each channel its own thread in the gauge service and replayed Tuesday. The website and the radio went at 02:31:01 and the sirens at 02:31:02; the SMS call hung on its own, timed out at 02:34:00 and went at 02:38:02 on its third try. Only the texts after the water. Then he replayed it with two things that had each happened before, though never together: the radio studio's line down until 02:32:30, and the gauge service restarting for an automatic update at 02:32:00. The radio thread was refused at 02:31:01 and 02:31:32, and its next try was due at 02:32:02. The restart came first. The retries lived in the gauge service's memory, and the gauge service sends only when the level crosses, so nothing went again. One alert lost. In February those two things did happen together. Quarrow Sound played music through the whole flood, and the presenter heard about it from a listener who rang in.
options.senior: Threads stop the channels waiting on each other, which fixes Tuesday. But the gauge service still owns every retry, in memory, so it has to stay up until the slowest channel succeeds; a restart, a crash or a deploy in that window loses whatever was still to send. And every new channel is a change to the gauge service. Hand the warning to something durable that keeps a copy per channel, and let the gauge service forget it.

options.text: Have each channel ask the gauge every 10 seconds whether a warning is up, and send it if so.
options.verdict: Trade-off: up to 10 seconds late, and polls all day
options.part2: Florimond turned the gauge service into something that only answers one question, is a warning up, and gave each channel a small poller that asks every 10 seconds, each at its own second, and sends the warning once. Tuesday replayed: the radio at 02:31:03, the website at 02:31:08, the sirens at 02:31:11, 99 seconds before the water. The SMS poller hung on its own and sent at 02:37:26 on its third try. A restart costs nothing; the warning is still there at the next poll. But four channels asking six times a minute is 34,560 polls a day, for a warning that comes on only a handful of nights, and adding the town's app as a fifth channel makes it 43,200. Each poller also has to remember, on its own, what it has already sent. The council's IT manager asked why the gauge was the busiest machine in the building on dry days.
options.senior: Polling makes each channel independent and lets the source forget, which is most of what you want. You pay with a delay of up to one interval and steady load that grows with every channel, almost all of it asking a question whose answer is no. A shorter interval cuts the delay and raises the load. Push the event once instead, and it arrives in about the time of one call.

options.text: Publish one warning to a topic; each channel gets its own queue, retries alone, fails alone.
options.part2: Florimond set up a warnings topic with four subscriptions, each a queue of its own, and a small worker per channel that takes the warning from its queue, calls its channel, and deletes the message only when the channel has answered. At 02:31:00 the gauge service now does one thing: it publishes the warning, and it is done. Tuesday replayed: the website and the radio at 02:31:01, the sirens at 02:31:02, 108 seconds before the water. The SMS worker hung on its own, timed out at 02:34:00, tried again at 02:34:30, and sent at 02:38:02 on its third try; nothing waited behind it. With the siren controller hanging instead, every other channel was out by 02:31:02. With the radio line down and the gauge service restarting at 02:32:00, the warning sat in the radio queue and went at 02:32:34 on the fourth try. In February the town added a push alert in its app as a fifth subscription; nobody touched the gauge service. In March the river crossed again at night. The mast across the road went off before I had got out of my chair.
options.senior: Publish the event once, and give each consumer its own queue, so each channel retries, waits and fails on its own, and a slow or dead one holds up nobody. The publisher forgets the warning once the topic has it; the queues keep it through restarts, and a dead-letter queue catches a channel that never recovers. Adding a channel is a new subscription, not a change to the publisher. The cost is more moving parts to watch, and a flow you can no longer read in one program.

sim.title: Run the Ollerby warning again
sim.lede: You're Ceinwen, replaying Tuesday from 02:30:00 to 02:45:00. The gauge crosses its warning level at 02:31:00, and the gauge service sends a warning only when the level crosses. Water reaches Doveridge Square at 02:32:50, from the square's own sensor. A call that works takes: SMS 2 s, website 1 s, sirens 2 s, radio 1 s. Calls to the channel that hangs, started before 02:37:00, wait the full 180-second timeout and fail; with the radio line down, radio calls before 02:32:30 are refused after 1 s. A failed try is tried again 30 s after it ends. The chain calls one channel at a time and retries failed ones after it. Parallel threads call all four at 02:31:00, and the gauge service keeps the retries in memory. Polling: each channel asks the gauge every 10 s, at its own second. Topic: one warning published at 02:31:00 and copied into a queue per channel; each channel's worker retries from its own queue. The gauge service can restart at 02:32:00 and is back at 02:32:20. The clock runs 20 times faster than real life. Click any box to see what it does.
sim.tryThis: Try this: press Skip to 02:45 as it is: the sirens at 02:34:03, 73 s after the water, and the texts at 02:38:02. Put the sirens first, then make the siren controller hang. Try parallel threads, then turn on the radio line down and the restart. Try polling and read the polls a day. Last, the topic: try every setting, then add the town app and watch the changes to the gauge service.

explain.oneLine: Nothing silenced the sirens. The gauge service called its four channels one after another and waited for each answer, so when the SMS provider hung, the sirens sat in line for the full 180-second timeout and sounded at 02:34:03, 73 seconds after the water reached the square.

steps.title: A chain of calls moves at the pace of its slowest link.
steps.text: Each channel was a call: the gauge service asked, then waited for the answer before asking the next. Four calls that work take 6 seconds in a row. One that hangs takes the whole timeout, 180 seconds, and every call behind it waits. The sirens didn't fail on Tuesday; they weren't asked until 02:34:01. Putting them first only changes which channel waits behind which: on a night the siren controller hangs, everything waits for it.

steps.title: Threads stop the waiting, not the owning.
steps.text: Calling all four at once sends the sirens at 02:31:02. But the gauge service still owns every channel's retry, in its memory, until the slowest channel succeeds. A restart in that window loses what was left: in the sim, the radio's try due at 02:32:02 dies with the restart at 02:32:00, and the gauge service, which sends only when the level crosses, never sends it again. Every new channel is also a change to the gauge service.

steps.title: Publish once, and let the topic make the copies.
steps.text: With pub/sub the gauge service publishes one warning to a topic and is finished. Each channel has a subscription, and the topic gives every subscription its own copy. That is fan-out: one message in, one copy per subscriber out. Make each subscription a queue, and each channel's worker takes the warning from its own queue, calls its channel, and deletes the message only when the channel answers. A hung SMS provider now holds up the SMS queue and nothing else.

steps.title: Each queue retries and fails alone.
steps.text: The queue keeps the message until it's deleted, so a failed try waits on that queue and is tried again, with a visibility timeout and a dead-letter queue like any other queue (Dead Letters). The gauge service can restart, crash or be deployed the moment it has published. A channel that never recovers ends up in its own dead-letter queue, with an alarm on it, instead of in a lost memory.

steps.title: The contract is the event, not the call.
steps.text: The publisher no longer knows its subscribers, so the event has to carry what they all need: an event contract, the fields every subscriber can rely on, such as the gauge, the level, the time it crossed and an event id. A subscriber that wants only some warnings sets a filter on its own subscription, instead of asking the publisher to change. Adding the town app is one more subscription. Each queue is at least once, so each worker should skip an event id it has already sent (At Least Once).

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn for the next high water. The gauge service publishes one warning to the warnings topic. The topic copies it into four queues, one each for SMS, website, sirens and radio, and each queue's worker calls its own channel. The website and the radio go at 02:31:01 and the sirens at 02:31:02. The SMS queue retries alone and its text goes at 02:38:02 on the third try.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for the next high water. The gauge service publishes one warning and is done. The topic copies it into a queue per channel, and each channel's worker calls its own channel. The SMS provider still hangs, but only the SMS queue waits: the sirens sound at 02:31:02, 108 seconds before the water.

fix.title: The fix: publish once, a queue per channel
fix.text: Create a warnings topic. Give each channel a subscription that delivers into a queue of its own, and a small worker that receives the warning from that queue, calls its channel, and deletes the message only when the channel has answered. The gauge service publishes one warning when the level crosses, with the gauge, the level, the time and an event id, and does nothing more. Give every queue a dead-letter queue with an alarm on its depth, and an alarm on the age of its oldest message, so a channel that is failing alone is still seen. Make each worker skip an event id it has already sent. To add a channel, add a subscription and a queue; the gauge service doesn't change.

limits: It doesn't make a hung channel faster. The SMS provider still hung until 02:37, and the texts still went at 02:38:02 in the sim; a second SMS provider, or a worker timeout shorter than 180 seconds, is what would change that.

Each queue is at least once, so a worker that crashes after its channel answers and before it deletes the message sends that warning again; each worker has to skip an event id it has already sent. And the flow is now spread over a topic, four queues and four workers: you can't read it in one program, so each queue's depth, its oldest message's age and its dead-letter queue need watching.

The publish itself must not be lost. If the gauge service crashes after deciding to warn and before the topic accepts the warning, no queue holds anything. Retry the publish until the topic accepts it, or write the warning to an outbox first (The Letter That Never Left).

head: Delivery
Good
Bad
rows: Simple; one program shows the whole flow.
Sirens at 02:34:03, 73 s after the water; all 4 channels after it.
3 channels still after the water; a siren hang puts all 4 after it.
Sirens at 02:31:02; only the texts after the water.
The gauge service holds every retry: a restart lost the radio alert. Each new channel changes it.
Sirens at 02:31:11; a restart loses nothing; no change to add a channel.
Up to 10 s late; 34,560 polls a day, 43,200 with the town app.
Sirens at 02:31:02; each channel retries alone; a restart loses nothing; a new channel is a new subscription.
More parts to run and watch; the flow isn't in one program; at least once, so workers skip repeats.

explain.seniorTake: When one event has several consumers, don't make the producer call them in turn and hold their retries. Publish the event once to a topic, give each consumer its own queue, and let each one retry, wait and fail alone, with its own dead-letter queue and alarm. The producer's job ends when the topic has the event, and its contract is the event's fields, not a list of who listens. Then say the cost out loud: more moving parts, at-least-once copies to skip, and a flow you see in monitoring rather than in one program.

realWorld.title: Martin Fowler, 2017: event notification
realWorld.text: In "What do you mean by 'Event-Driven'?", Martin Fowler describes event notification as a system sending event messages to notify other systems of a change in its domain, and says that a key element of event notification is that the source system doesn't really care much about the response. That is the gauge service after the fix: it publishes the warning and waits for no channel.

realWorld.title: Fowler's warning about the flow
realWorld.text: The same article warns that it's very easy to make nicely decoupled systems with event notification, without realizing that you're losing sight of that larger-scale flow, and that often the only way to figure out this flow is from monitoring a live system. It is why the fix puts an alarm on every queue.

realWorld.title: Amazon SNS to SQS: fanning out
realWorld.text: AWS's page on fanning out Amazon SNS notifications to Amazon SQS queues says that when you subscribe an Amazon SQS queue to an Amazon SNS topic, you can publish a message to the topic and Amazon SNS sends an Amazon SQS message to the subscribed queue, and that the messages also persist in an Amazon SQS queue for other applications to process later. The same page says SNS sends to multiple subscribers through a push mechanism, which removes the need to check or poll for updates.

realWorld.title: Filters belong to the subscription
realWorld.text: SNS's message filtering page says that by default a topic subscriber receives every message published to the topic, and that to receive only a subset of the messages, a subscriber must assign a filter policy to the topic subscription. The publisher doesn't change.

realWorld.title: EventBridge rules
realWorld.text: EventBridge's rules page says a rule specifies which events to send to which targets, and a single rule can send an event to multiple targets, which then run in parallel.

asked: How do you stop one slow consumer slowing the rest?
interview.answer: Start by separating the thing that decides to notify from the things that deliver. The producer, say an order service or a sensor, publishes one event to a topic, with a stable contract: what happened, when, the fields the channels need, and an event id. Each delivery channel, email, SMS, push, webhooks, has its own subscription into its own queue and its own workers. That's fan-out: one event in, one copy per subscriber out, and each copy retries, waits and fails on its own, so a slow email provider backs up the email queue and nothing else. Size each worker's timeout to its channel, put a dead-letter queue and an alarm on every queue, and alarm on the oldest message's age so a channel failing alone is still seen. Subscribers that want some events use a filter on their subscription, and a new channel is a new subscription, with no change to the producer. Then the costs: queues are at least once, so workers skip event ids they've already sent; the publish has to be made safe, with retries or an outbox; and the end-to-end flow lives in monitoring, not in one program. Calling the channels in a chain, or in threads inside the producer, keeps all the retries in one process, and a restart there loses them.

The river height at which the office warns the town. On Tuesday the Quarrow crossed it at 02:31:00.
Florimond's program that reads the gauge and, when the river crosses the warning level, sends the warning out. It sends only on the crossing.
One way of warning people. Ollerby has four: SMS, the website, the sirens and the local radio. The town app becomes a fifth.
The system that sounds the town's sirens when it is called. 2 s when it works.
Ollerby's local radio station. Its alert line breaks into whatever is on air with the warning.
The lowest part of Ollerby, where people park overnight. Its own level sensor saw water on the paving at 02:32:50.
A sensor that records when water reaches it. The one in Doveridge Square gives the sim its water time.
One program asking another to do something and waiting for the answer before it goes on.
Calls made one after another, each waiting for the last to answer. Ollerby's: SMS, website, sirens, radio.
A call that gets no answer and no error, so the caller waits until its timeout. On Tuesday the SMS provider hung until 02:37.
Making several calls at once, each in its own thread inside one program, so none waits for another.
A way for programs to talk where a publisher sends a message to a topic, and every subscriber to that topic gets its own copy. The publisher doesn't know who they are.
Hand one message to a topic, which delivers it to every subscriber. The publisher's job ends there.
A named place for one kind of message, like warnings. Subscribers sign up to it; each message published to it is copied to all of them.
A program, or queue, that receives a copy of every message published to a topic it has signed up to.
A subscriber's sign-up to a topic, saying where its copies go, such as a queue, and optionally a filter.
One message in, one copy per subscriber out. With a queue per subscriber, each copy is retried and fails on its own.
Each alert channel's subscription delivers into its own queue, read by its own worker, so a slow channel backs up only its own queue.
Building a system around events: things that happened are published, and other parts react to them, rather than the source calling each one.
Martin Fowler's name for a system sending events to tell others something changed, without caring much about their response.
The fields an event always carries and what they mean, which every subscriber relies on. Changing it means warning the subscribers.
A unique id carried in an event, so a worker can tell a repeat of an event it has already handled.
A rule on a subscription that lets through only some messages, such as severe warnings only, without changing the publisher.
Amazon SNS's name for a subscription's filter: a JSON object saying which messages that subscriber receives.

In Amazon EventBridge, a rule that matches events and sends them to one or more targets.

A small program that asks a source on a timer whether anything is new. In the sim, one per channel, every 10 s.

Software updating itself on a schedule and restarting, without anyone on the desk doing it.

Tries after the first, added up across every channel.
The step in an online shop where the customer pays and the order is placed.
A call one system makes to a web address another system gave it, to tell it something happened.
A chat app many teams use for work; alerts are often posted into its channels.
The SOC 2 availability criteria: evidence that a system stays available as its commitments say.

atWork: Look for one event that several things react to, and check whether the thing that noticed it calls each of them itself. A common incident is a checkout that waited on a slow email service before confirming orders: the order request sent the confirmation email inline, the email provider slowed down, and checkouts timed out though the payments had gone through. Read-only access is enough. Find where your system sends a notification, a receipt or an audit record: is it a call inside the request, a loop over channels, threads in one process, or a publish to a topic or an EventBridge rule? If it's a call, what is its timeout, and what waits behind it? Where do the retries live: in that process's memory, or on a queue that survives a restart? For each subscriber, is there a queue of its own, a dead-letter queue and an alarm on it? Build Night N3 builds alerts that fan out to email, Slack and webhooks: this is the shape it needs. In LATENT, Keeping It Fresh (a3e09) sends its change feed to its readers the same way. If your company is pursuing SOC 2 with availability in scope, criterion A1 asks for evidence that the system meets its availability commitments; a test showing that one dead alert channel doesn't stop the others, with an alarm on each queue, is that kind of evidence.

recall.prompt: Your shop's checkout service takes the payment, then calls the email service to send a confirmation, then the warehouse service, then the analytics service, and each must answer before the next is called; only then does it tell the customer the order is placed. One evening the email service slows to 30 seconds a call, and checkouts start timing out, though the payments went through. What is going wrong, and how would you redesign it?

keyIdeas.idea: The calls run as a chain, so the slow email call holds up everything behind it, including the reply to the customer
Publish one order-placed event to a topic, and let each service subscribe to it
Give each consumer its own queue, so it retries and fails alone and the checkout answers at once

recall.model: The checkout calls the services in a chain and waits for each answer before the next, so the slow email service holds up the warehouse call, the analytics call and the reply to the customer; enough of that and checkouts time out even though the payment worked. Only the payment has to happen before you answer. Publish one order-placed event to a topic and answer the customer. Give email, warehouse and analytics each their own queue subscribed to the topic, with a worker that retries from that queue, so a slow email service only backs up emails: each consumer retries and fails alone, with its own dead-letter queue and alarm. Each worker skips an event id it has already handled, because the queues are at least once.

recall.prompt: Ollerby's gauge service is changed to call all four channels at once, each in its own thread. Which failure does that design still have?
options: A hung SMS call delays the sirens by the full 180-second timeout.
A restart of the gauge service loses any retry it was still holding in memory.
Each channel asks the gauge 8,640 times a day.
The sirens can sound only after the website has been updated.
recall.why: Threads stop the channels waiting on each other, so the sirens go at 02:31:02 even while the SMS call hangs. But every retry still lives in the gauge service's memory. In the sim, with the radio line down, the radio's try due at 02:32:02 is lost when the gauge service restarts at 02:32:00, and because it sends only when the level crosses, nothing sends it again. Polling is the design that asks the gauge 8,640 times a day per channel.

recall.prompt: Your order service publishes order events to a topic, and four services each read it through a queue. The fraud team wants only orders over 500 dollars, and a new loyalty service wants every order. A developer proposes adding an if statement to the order service that sends big orders straight to fraud, and another call for loyalty. What do you suggest instead?

keyIdeas.idea: Put a filter on the fraud team's subscription instead of changing the publisher
The loyalty service gets its own queue and subscription; the order service doesn't change
Both rely on the event contract: the order event must carry the amount as a field subscribers can use

recall.model: Leave the order service alone; not knowing its subscribers is the point of the topic. The fraud team adds a filter policy to its own subscription that matches only orders whose amount is over 500, so the topic sends it just those. The loyalty service gets a new queue and a new subscription to the topic, and starts receiving every order; the publisher doesn't change. Both depend on the event contract: the order event has to carry the amount as a field or attribute, and nobody can rename or drop that field without warning its subscribers.

recall.prompt: In the sim's polling mode on Tuesday's night, why do the sirens sound at 02:31:11 rather than 02:31:02?
options: The siren poller asks the gauge every 10 s at its own second, so it saw the warning 9 s after the crossing, and the call took 2 s.
The SMS poller hung, and the siren poller had to wait until it finished.
The gauge service called the website first.
Copying the warning into the queues took 9 seconds.
recall.why: With polling nobody is told; each channel finds out on its next poll. The siren poller asks at 9 seconds past each 10, so the first poll after the 02:31:00 crossing is 02:31:09, and the siren call takes 2 s: 02:31:11. Each poller is independent, so the hung SMS poller holds up nobody. The delay is up to one polling interval, and the price is steady load: 34,560 polls a day for four channels.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 4 months later. The topic and the four queues have held through two high waters; every channel has gone out on time, and the hung SMS provider held up nobody. Then in June Quarrow Sound moved its alert line to a new address and told nobody. At the next warning the radio worker's calls failed, try after try, and the message ended up in the radio's dead-letter queue. The other three channels went out within seconds. The screen Florimond watches showed the topic healthy all night. Nobody knew the radio hadn't warned until the station manager rang the next morning to ask why the river had been on the news and not on her station.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. How did the radio fail without anyone noticing, and what should change?

keyIdeas.idea: Each channel fails alone, so the publisher and the topic look healthy while one channel quietly fails; nothing upstream sees it
Put an alarm on each channel's dead-letter queue depth and on its oldest message's age
Check delivery end to end: a test warning through every channel, and confirm each channel actually answered

coldCase.model: The design did what it promised: the radio failed alone, so nothing else waited for it. That is also why nobody saw it. The gauge service had published and forgotten, and the topic had handed every copy to its queue, so both looked healthy; the only place the failure showed was the radio's own dead-letter queue, and nothing watched it. Put an alarm on each channel's dead-letter queue, so one message there wakes the desk, and on the age of each queue's oldest message, so a channel that keeps failing is seen within a minute or two. Then test the whole path: send a test warning through every channel on a schedule, and confirm each channel answered, so a moved address is found on a dry night instead of a wet one. Once the address is fixed, the message in the dead-letter queue can be redriven, though by then the warning may be stale.
